opus-5.5.text:
I do, but with some nuance. I've spent most of my career building simulators, so I'm obviously biased, but I think the honest answer is that sim-to-real works extremely well in some domains and is still really hard in others.

Think about locomotion. Training a quadruped or even a humanoid to walk in simulation and then deploying it on real hardware works remarkably well now. The physics of rigid bodies and contact is understood well enough, and with domain randomization you can cover the gap: you randomize friction, mass, motor latency, and the policy learns to be robust to all of it. The real world just becomes one more sample from the distribution.

Where it gets harder is manipulation, especially with deformable things like cloth, cables, liquids, or food. Contact-rich, soft-body interaction is very expensive to simulate accurately, and small errors compound. Rendering is another gap: if your policy depends on vision, the simulated images have to look close enough to real camera data, and that's still not trivial, although neural rendering is helping a lot.

So my view is that simulation is a fantastic tool for getting scale. Real-world data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous to collect, while in simulation you can run thousands of environments in parallel on a GPU. But I don't think it's simulation versus real data. The winning recipe will probably be lots of simulated data to learn the broad structure, plus a smaller amount of real data to close the last gap.

And honestly, that's one reason I care so much about making simulators faster and easier to program. If the tools improve, the set of problems where sim-to-real "just works" keeps growing.

r002.rationale: It mentions simulation-to-reality gaps in contact physics and rendering, but does not identify mismatches in boundary conditions.

r003.rationale: It describes simulation’s strengths and limits across domains, but does not state that a simulation-pretrained model is limited to cases its simulator can provide.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I do believe in it—but I think the honest answer is "yes, with a lot of asterisks."

Let me explain where I'm coming from. I spent years building Taichi, which is basically a programming language for physical simulation—fluids, soft bodies, deformable materials, that kind of thing. One of the things we did early on was make these simulators differentiable, so you could backpropagate through the physics itself. And the whole motivation was sim-to-real: if you can simulate a robot or a material accurately enough, and you can take gradients through that simulation, you can learn controllers and policies in the computer and then deploy them in the real world. So I'm deeply invested in the idea.

Where I've become more careful is on the word "accurately enough." The gap between simulation and reality isn't one gap, it's many. There's the physics gap—your material model is an approximation, your contact model is an approximation, friction is never quite right. There's the sensing gap—real cameras have noise, motion blur, weird lighting. And there's the modeling gap—there are things in the real world you simply didn't think to put in the simulator at all. Rigid body stuff, locomotion, those have worked surprisingly well because the physics is relatively well understood. But the moment you get into deformables, fluids, cloth, granular materials, the simulation itself becomes the bottleneck, and that's exactly where I spent most of my research effort.

So my view is that sim-to-real is less a yes/no belief and more an engineering discipline. You need fast simulation so you can generate a lot of diverse data. You need domain randomization so the model doesn't overfit to your particular approximations. And ideally you need the simulator to be differentiable or at least tunable, so you can close the loop—take real-world observations and fit the simulator back to them, what people call real-to-sim. The teams I've seen succeed treat the simulator as a living thing that gets calibrated against reality, not a static oracle.

And honestly, what makes me optimistic right now is that the data generation side is finally getting cheap. GPU simulation, differentiable physics, neural surrogates for the expensive parts—these have made it possible to generate orders of magnitude more varied experience than you could ever collect on a physical robot. So, do I believe in it? Yes. But I believe in it the way you believe in a tool, not a miracle. The simulation is only as good as the effort you put into making it match the world.

astra-6.text:
Yes, I do, but I don’t think simulation has to reproduce the real world perfectly to be useful. The question is whether it captures the things that matter for the task you’re trying to learn.

For example, you can train a model across a range of simulated conditions—different friction, different masses, different sensor noise—so it doesn’t depend on one very specific environment. Then you test it in the real world and use what you learn to improve the simulation or adapt the model.

So I see simulation as a way to do a lot of the learning cheaply and safely. You still need real-world feedback. The interesting part is figuring out how to combine the two.

sol-6.1.text:
Yes, I do, but I think the key question is how well the simulation captures what matters for the task. A simulator doesn’t need to reproduce every detail of the real world. It needs to be accurate enough that the skills a model learns will transfer.

You can also vary the conditions during training—things like friction, lighting, or object properties—so the model doesn’t depend on one very specific setup. But you still have to test it in the real world and use those results to improve the simulation. I see it as a loop between simulation and reality, rather than expecting simulation alone to solve everything.
